--- title: "GitHub and Hosting Quarto Documents Online" subtitle: "PSYC 6019-A01 / PSYC 6022-A01
2026-11-24 | Lab 14" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true slide-number: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss width: 1200 execute: echo: true dpi: 600 freeze: auto knitr: opts_chunk: dev: svg --- ## Outline - GitHub basics - Quarto websites - Quarto publishing ::: {.cell} ::: ## Today's Resources :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} ### Git Basics [Happy Git with R](https://happygitwithr.com/) This is where I learned how to get started with Git and GitHub! ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ### Quarto Websites ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ### Quarto Publishing ::: :::: I will be heavily pulling from these resources in these slides. Relevant references will be in the footer of the slide. ## Goals for Today We are going to be covering a lot today! My main goal is to get everyone using the basic functionalities that allow you to host Quarto on GitHub. There may be details or terminology that feel confusing---that is OK. There is lots of background information and context that we won't cover today. The resources provided have much more detail. I encourage you to read through them at your own pace to fill in the gaps of what we will skip today. ::: subsubpoint ○ Probably especially [Happy Git with R](https://happygitwithr.com/) ::: # Git and GitHub Basics ## About Git Git is a version control system ::: subpoint ○ Originally made for software developers to manage large codebases ::: "Manages the "manages the evolution of a set of files---called a **repository** or **repo**---in a sane, highly structured way." (Bryan, 2017, p. 2) Now often used for researchers to manage their coding / data work. ::: subsubpoint ○ Many of the functionalities map over well ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ We often have a collection of code files, figures, data, etc that can run rampant if untamed... ::: ## About Git Without vs. with Git changes ![](../media/lab_14/diy_vs_git.png) ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Why Git](https://happygitwithr.com/big-picture#why-git) and [Excuse me, do you have a moment to talk about version control?](https://peerj.com/preprints/3159v2/) ::: ## About GitHub GitHub is a helpful **user interface** to Git (similar to how RStudio is a user interface to R) and provides a **hosting service** for our projects. ::: subpoint ○ Allows other people to easily look at the files, suggest changes, sync up themselves. ::: ::: subpoint ○ Offers controls of who can see and edit the project ::: If you do something silly to your files locally, you can always reset if you have been pushing to GitHub! ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Why GitHub](https://happygitwithr.com/big-picture#why-github) and [Excuse me, do you have a moment to talk about version control?](https://peerj.com/preprints/3159v2/) ::: ## Benefits of Git / GitHub ::: footer [Happy Git with R: What is the payoff?](https://happygitwithr.com/big-picture#what-is-the-payoff) and [Excuse me, do you have a moment to talk about version control?](https://peerj.com/preprints/3159v2/) ::: ## Getting Started In order to get all this working, we have a couple steps ahead of us: ::: subpoint ○ Register for a GitHub account (free) ::: ::: subpoint ○ Install Git ::: ::: subpoint ○ Install a local Git client ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ Will be a friendly interface to working with Git on our end ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ An alternative is working on the command line ::: ::: subpoint ○ Connect Git and RStudio ::: ::: subpoint ○ Confirm we can interact with Git! ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ We can create a practice repository to do this ::: ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Is it going to hurt?](https://happygitwithr.com/big-picture#is-it-going-to-hurt) and [Excuse me, do you have a moment to talk about version control?](https://peerj.com/preprints/3159v2/) ::: ## I. GitHub Account Create an account on [github.com](https://github.com/){target="_blank"} Jenny Bryan's advice on usernames (paraphrased): ::: blockquote - Incorporate your actual name! People like to know who they’re dealing with. Also makes your username easier for people to guess or remember. - Reuse your username from other contexts, e.g., Twitter or Slack. - Pick a username you will be comfortable revealing to your future boss. - Shorter is better than longer. - Make it timeless. Don’t highlight your current university, employer, or place of residence, e.g. JennyFromTheBlock. - Avoid the use of upper vs. lower case to separate words. We highly recommend all lowercase. A better strategy for word separation is to use a hyphen -. ::: You can always change your username later. ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Register a GitHub Account](https://happygitwithr.com/github-acct#github-acct) ::: ## II. Install Git Do you have Git already? Check in the RStudio Terminal. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ```{.bash filename="Terminal"} which git ## /usr/bin/git ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ```{.bash filename="Terminal"} git --version ## git version 2.50.1 ``` ::: :::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="66%"} ### Windows Install [Git for Windows](https://git-for-windows.github.io/) ::: {.blockquote style="font-size:85%"} **NOTE**: When asked about “Adjusting your PATH environment”, make sure to select “Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software”. Otherwise, we believe it is good to accept the defaults. Note that RStudio for Windows prefers for Git to be installed below C:/Program Files and this appears to be the default. This implies, for example, that the Git executable on my Windows system is found at C:/Program Files/Git/bin/git.exe. Unless you have specific reasons to otherwise, follow this convention. ::: ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} ### macOS Go to the shell (Terminal) and enter these commands: ```{.bash filename="Terminal"} git --version git config ``` Click "Install" ::: :::: ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Install Git](https://happygitwithr.com/install-git#install-git) ::: ## III. Introduce Yourself to Git :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### In the Shell ``` git config --global user.name "Jane Doe" git config --global user.email "jane@example.com" git config --global --list ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### In R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## install.packages("usethis") library(usethis) use_git_config(user.name = "Jane Doe", user.email = "jane@example.org") ``` ::: ::: :::: **Username**: Can be your GitHub username, can also be your name **Email**: **Needs to be** the same email you used for your GitHub account ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Introduce yourself to Git](https://happygitwithr.com/hello-git#hello-git) ::: ## IV. Install a Git Client Having a user interface can be a smoother way of interacting with Git, especially when starting out. There are options, but I recommend (and use) [GitKraken](https://www.gitkraken.com/). ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Install a Git client](https://happygitwithr.com/git-client) ::: ## V. Get Everything Connected When we need to talk to a remote (e.g., on the Internet, including our own) GitHub repository, we need to include credentials that prove we are a specific GitHub user, allowed to do what we're trying to do. ::: subpoint ○ In the olden days, we could do this by entering our passwords. GitHub no longer considers password secure enough---so we just need to do a little fiddling to set these credentials up. ::: How do we do this? Two options: ::: subpoint ○ **HTTPS**: recommended by *Happy Git with R*, what we are going to do ::: ::: subpoint ○ **SSH**: an alternative method. Feel free to read more [here](https://happygitwithr.com/ssh-keys) ::: Instead of a password, we will use a **Personal Access Token (PAT)**. We will go to GitHub, ask it to generate a **PAT**, and then tell RStudio the **PAT** to connect RStudio with GitHub. ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Personal access token for HTTPS](https://happygitwithr.com/https-pat) ::: ## V. Get Everything Connected 1. Go to [https://github.com/settings/tokens](https://github.com/settings/tokens) and click "Generate Token" From R, you could also do: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} usethis::create_github_token() ``` ::: In the settings, Jenny recommends selecting "repo," "user," and "workflow." 2. Copy the generated PAT 3. Set your Git credentials in R with the following code and pasting your PAT. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gitcreds::gitcreds_set() ``` ::: ``` ? Enter password or token: ghp_xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx -> Adding new credentials... -> Removing credentials from cache... -> Done. ``` ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Personal access token for HTTPS](https://happygitwithr.com/https-pat) ::: ## VI. Connect to GitHub Let's make sure we can **push** and **pull** from GitHub to our computer! 1. Let's make a repo on GitHub ::: subpoint ○ Repositories > New ::: ::: blockquote How to fill this in: - Repository template: No template. - Repository name: myrepo or whatever you wish (we’ll delete this soon). - Description: “Repository for testing my Git/GitHub setup” or similar. It’s nice to have something here, so you’ll see it appear in the README. - Public. - Initialize this repository with: Add a README file. Click the big green button that says “Create repository”. Now click the big green button that says “<> Code”. Copy a clone URL to your clipboard. If you’re taking our default advice, copy the HTTPS URL. But if you’re opting for SSH, then make sure to copy the SSH URL. ::: I recommend trying a public repo, but private is an option too. ::: footer [Happy Git with R: Connect to GitHub](https://happygitwithr.com/push-pull-github) ::: ## VI. Connect to GitHub 2. Clone the repo onto your computer This is like making our own, local version of this repository, which is currently empty with just a `README` file. ::: subpoint ○ Copy the URL of the repository (e.g., `https://github.com/username/my-repo`) ::: ::: subpoint ○ Open GitKraken, File > Clone repo... ::: ::: subpoint ○ Clone with URL ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ Where to clone to: pick a location for a new folder on your computer. I'm going to do mine next to my `live-coding` folder for this class. ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ URL: paste in the repository URL ::: ::: subpoint ○ Clone the repo! ::: ## VI. Connect to GitHub Let's turn this newly-created folder into an R Project, like we made for this class. ::: subpoint ○ Open RStudio, File > New Project > Existing Directory ::: ::: subpoint ○ Navigate to the new repo folder ::: We now have *new files* in our *local* version of this repository: an .Rproj file, and a .gitignore file. Let's get these onto the **remote** (GitHub's version) of the repo. In RStudio, we can use the Git pane. ::: subpoint ○ Check the "Staged" box next to each file ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ This is telling RStudio which files we want to add to the remote ::: ::: subpoint ○ Click the "Commit" button ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ This is like putting all the added files into an envelope to send to Git ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ Add a commit message: a short description of what is changing with this commit ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ Click the "Commit" button ::: ::: subpoint ○ Click the "Pull" button ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ This is bringing down any new changes on the remote's version. This is unnecessary in our example, because there's no one else interacting with the remote. But, it's a good habit to build for collaboration with Git. ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ `Already up to date` ::: ::: subpoint ○ Click the "Push" button ::: ::: subsubpoint ○ This is sending off our commit to the remote! ::: ## VI. Connect to GitHub Let's check the remote. Can we see the new files? We have successfully **pushed** our changes in the directory to the **remote**. Now we can practice **pulling** changes. Modify the `README.md` file by clicking the edit button (little pencil) on the website. Go back to RStudio, and click "Pull" to bring the changed `README.md` to your local version. We have now finished setup :) ## What's Next? We have successfully been able to edit files and **push** / **pull** them to / from GitHub. We will now do this with Quarto files, so we can have a live-hosted Quarto website on our GitHub page! We will practice pushing and pulling (mostly pushing) to / from Git throughout our process of creating the website. ## Appendix: From Local to Git Generally, starting a project by creating a repo on Git and then adding files is a smooth way to work. But, you may have an existing project on your computer and want to now host it on GitHub. This matches the ["Existing project, GitHub last"](https://happygitwithr.com/existing-github-last) page in the [Happy Git with R](https://happygitwithr.com/) book. Refer to it for how to implement this! ::: footer [Happy Git with R: "Existing project, GitHub last](https://happygitwithr.com/existing-github-last) ::: # Quarto Websites ## Quarto Websites So far, we've mostly been using Quarto documents (single HTML files). Today, we are going to make a Quarto website. What is a Quarto website? A Quarto website is just a way of organizing multiple Quarto documents. Instead of just having one page to scroll through, now we can have multiple. By default, will have navigation features set up to help move throughout your website. Why website instead of a document? Websites allow you to have more than one page. You can have a website with just one page if you want, and then you will always have the flexibility of adding more (e.g., a new analysis, a Quarto slide deck for a presentation) ::: footer [Quarto Websites](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) ::: ## Quarto Website Examples Small gallery of 2--3 Quarto websites. One being the class site. ## Creating a Website Let's turn our newly created Git repository into a Quarto website. One way to create a Quarto website is in RStudio, File > New Project > New Directory > Quarto Website But we already have a directory---our local version of the Git repo! Luckily, all we need is two things: a Quarto file named `index.qmd` (to be our "homepage"), and a config file named `_quarto.yml` (this just tells Quarto to render as a website! And, we can specify settings for the whole site). ::: footer [Quarto Websites: Creating a Website](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) ::: ## Creating a Website Let's add a Quarto document `index.qmd`, like we've made Quarto documents before. Next, let's create the `_quarto.yml` file. To do this, I usually click File > New File > Text File, and then save it and type in the name with the file extension specified. ::: subpoint ○ Check the Files pane to make sure it did not add `.txt` ::: Now, our config file needs some stuff. I usually go to the [Quarto Websites](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/) page and copy the default config file, provided under [Config File](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/#config-file). ## Default Config File I've also included the default config file here.
```{=html} ```
::: footer [Quarto Websites: Config File](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/#config-file)0Regression%20Diagnostics/Lecture%2027%20Regression%20Diagnostics.html#/multicolinearity) accessed on 2026-11-19. ::: ## Creating a Website Now let's render our site. The top right says "today", and the "about.qmd" link does nothing. These are things we can adjust in our `_quarto.yml` or fix by adding a new page! Changing title to "My Website" :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"} project: type: website website: title: "My Website" navbar: left: - href: index.qmd text: Home - about.qmd format: html: theme: cosmo css: styles.css toc: true ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} `navbar` is specifying Navigation Bar settings, and `left` means it is located on the top-left of the page. `- href` is specifying a link to a page with the **path** to that file from the project root. By default, it uses the `title` specified in the Quarto document's YAML. You can manually specify a title putting `text: New Title` below the link (`href`). See more about navigation at [Quarto Websites: Website Navigation](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-navigation.html) We don't have an `about.qmd` right now, but we can create one! ::: :::: ## Next Steps We have successfully created a Quarto website that has a couple pages. You don't need to wait until your website is fully set-up to start pushing things to Git. It's good practice to "commit early and often." Now, let's get our website onto GitHub!!! # Quarto on GitHub ## Quarto on GitHub The Quarto docs provide excellent documentation on hosting your website on GitHub at [Publishing: GitHub Pages](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html){target="_blank"}. GitHub Pages is GitHub's website hosting service. It is free, and compatible with hosting HTML pages made from Quarto! We will follow its instructions (publishing way 1) together. ::: subpoint ○ I refer back to these instructions just about every time I'm putting a Quarto website online. There's no need to memorize any of this. ::: ## Render to `docs` So far, when we render our Quarto documents, the outputted HTML any any files (those little `page_files` folders) go into the *same directory* as the Quarto document. For websites, it can be helpful to keep the **source** and the **output** separate: so GitHub Pages knows what to use as the actual website content (the rendered HTML, not the Quarto source code). We will modify our `_quarto.yml` to use `docs` as the `output-dir`. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ```{.yaml filename="_quarto.yml"} project: type: website output-dir: docs ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} And now we can rerender our site. The HTML files will all go into a `docs` folder, and we can delete the old `page_files` folders in the main directory. ::: :::: ## Last Details GitHub Pages (by default) will do additional processing of the HTML we ask it to host via Jekyll (GitHub Pages' default website-creation tool). We can ask it not do this by adding a file `.nojekyll`. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Windows ```{.bash filename="Terminal"} touch .nojekyll ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### macOS ```{.bash filename="Terminal"} copy NUL .nojekyll ``` ::: :::: Now, let's get all these changes onto the remote repository! ## Using GitKraken So far, we've used RStudio's Git pane, but GitKraken is a nicer way of interacting with Git. When you open the folder in GitKraken (may already be open from cloning), you can see all the commits made so far. You can stage changes one-by-one (like clicking the checkbox in RStudio), or Stage All Changes. Add a commit message, and commit. Pull, push. ## Hosting the Website We now should be able to see all the changes (`.qmd` files, `docs` folder, etc.) on the online version of the repository. Let's now get the website content rendering as webpages! In the repository, go to Settings > Pages. Under Branch, switch `None` to `main`. Then, switch `/ (root)` to `/docs` and click Save. This tells GitHub Pages host use the HTML in the `docs` folder. You should see "Your GitHub Pages site is currently being built from the /docs folder in the main branch." After a minute or two, refresh the page. You should see Your site is live at URL. Go to that URL! Your site is now live on the internet. Anyone with that link will be able to view the content. ## Adding to Our Website Let's also add an `analysis.qmd` document that has some brief analyses of the `palmerpenguins` data and render. Then, let's commit and push those changes to get our analysis live on GitHub!

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
